newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says seeks to revive hostage release plan.
newsitem.headline: Peru says seeks to revive hostage release plan.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori sought to recapture the initiative in a propaganda war with Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima and said his government wanted to reestablish a timetable agreed 10 days ago to end the crisis.
"I would say we are looking for more favourable conditions allowing this contact to happen," Fujimori said in an interview with CNN on Wednesday.

Fujimori's appointed negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, spoke face-to-face with Nestor Cerpa, the leader of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels in the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador on Dec. 28. He won the release of 20 hostages but has not returned since.

Fujimori said an impromptu news conference by the rebels on New Year's Eve -- made possible by a sudden rush into the residence by about 20 journalists during a photo opportunity -- had thrown accords reached by Palermo and Cerpa off track.

"Unfortunately there was an unforeseen news conference ... when we had a whole working timetable with this MRTA group," Fujimori said. "The news conference was going to take place with some concessions on their part but it was brought forward without any ... this threw the process off a little and now we are in the middle of evaluating it," he said.

Fujimori repeated he would not grant the rebels' main demand, that he release some 400 of their jailed colleagues, and said if any of the hostages were hurt the government would consider using force to end the crisis.

Otherwise, he said, an agreement had been reached to form a "commission of guarantors" who would oversee a peaceful end to the stand-off. "Where we have left a door open is with regard to the creation of a group of guarantors and to the peaceful ways out that could exist and that would be studied with this group of guarantors," Fujimori said. He gave no other details.

With no concrete developments in the deadlocked crisis since New Year's Day, a relaxed and joking Fujimori led an election-style tour through Lima's poor neighbourhoods to prove the rebel siege had not paralysed the country.

"This is a great demonstration ... in favour of the government, in favour of peace, and against violence," said Fujimori, clad in jeans and a white casual shirt as he headed a caravan of hundreds of journalists and officials.
The visit contrasted starkly with Fujimori's previous wall of silence and grim expression during his few public appearances since the crisis began.
To cries of "We are with you" from the crowds who came out to greet him, Fujimori again lambasted as "terrorists" the MRTA rebels. "There is no MRTA follower here," Fujimori said.
Fujimori also urged Japanese firms not to give in to demands for ransom for their employees inside the residence.
Although the MRTA has in the past kidnapped businessmen and politicians to raise money, there has been no evidence that this was their aim in the current crisis.
Underscoring the government's new propaganda offensive, diplomats abroad and public relations officials in Peru were told to begin damage-limitation publicity campaigns.

"Much of the news coverage paints the MRTA as if they were good boys, idealistic and romantic, when in fact they are terrorists, and that's how the Peruvian people regard them," said one Peruvian diplomat in another Latin American capital during a briefing with journalists.

Beatriz Boza, head of the government's public relations unit Promperu, told reporters that despite the crisis, Peru had received a total $1.5 billion in foreign investment and loans since the Dec. 17 takeover.

Until Wednesday, the MRTA had been overshadowing the government with propaganda tools ranging from cardboard placards and megaphones to daily updating of Internet pages and an international spokesman on call in Germany.

As well as abandoning its previous silence, the government also took a tougher approach on Wednesday to journalists covering the crisis, detaining a reporter and a translator working for Japan's TV Asahi. The pair sneaked past police on Tuesday for a two-hour meeting with the MRTA.
Peruvian anti-terrorism police confiscated the pair's notebooks and cameras and said they would be held for at least five days while authorities decide whether to press charges.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi both condemned the pair's action as likely to jeopardise efforts to solve the crisis.
The MRTA rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took about 500 hostages including ambassadors and senior Peruvian government officials. Most of them were later released.

Former Peruvian showgirl Susy Diaz, now a prominent legislator and singer, offered to swap places with the hostages and called on the rebels to "make love, not war". There was no immediate response from the MRTA or the government.
